title: What is RAG in AI? A plain-English guide for marketers
content:
More of your audience now gets answers from AI instead of a list of links. So when someone asks an assistant about your category, the response draws on sources you may never even see, and your brand either shows up in it — or doesn’t.
That shift changes what AI in content marketing asks of you. Writing a strong page used to be the finish line. Now you also need to know how AI systems find, select, and cite pages, and that starts with a question many marketers haven’t had a reason to ask yet: what is RAG in AI?
Pew Research Center looked at this behavior in a 2025 analysis of 900 U.S. adults’ browsing data . Users clicked a traditional search result on 8% of visits when Google showed an AI summary, compared with 15% of visits without one. Fewer clicks means the answer itself carries more weight, and so do the sources behind it — the pages a system pulls from can shape what it says about you.
This guide explains RAG in plain language, starting with what it means for your marketing and then covering how it works. You’ll leave with a checklist for making your content easier for retrieval systems to use.
One caveat up front: retrieval-friendly content can improve machine accessibility, but it doesn’t guarantee retrieval or citation.
RAG in AI is a method that retrieves relevant information from an external knowledge base before a model generates an answer. The name stands for retrieval-augmented generation, and it also shows up in conversations about GenAI RAG setups. In each case, RAG augments the model’s prompt with retrieved source material, which improves answer grounding.
Without RAG, a language model answers from what it absorbed during training. With RAG, it checks a source first. That source can be a help center, a product database, or a set of company documents, and the answer reflects what the model finds there.
RAG matters because it connects AI answers to source material, and your content can be that source material.
A standard large language model (LLM) generates answers from patterns it learned during training. That knowledge has a cutoff date and doesn’t include your latest pricing page, product launch, or help article. RAG fills that gap. The system retrieves relevant context from an external knowledge base, then uses it to write the answer.
Answer engines retrieve and cite sources differently, so you can’t predict outcomes for any single platform. What you can do is make your content easier for machines to read, which is the focus of the sections below.
RAG works in three steps: retrieve, augment, generate. If you want the broader picture of what’s happening inside these systems first, our guide on how AI works covers the fundamentals.
Here’s a marketer-friendly example. Say your company has a help article about resetting a password. Behind the scenes, a RAG system prepares that article in advance:
When someone asks, “How do I reset my password?”, the system finds the closest-matching chunks, adds them to the prompt, and generates an answer. If the system is built to show sources, it can cite the help article.
Text version of the workflow: question comes in, the system retrieves matching chunks from the knowledge base, adds them to the prompt, the model generates an answer, and the answer can link back to the source.
Retrieval-augmented generation is a method that combines a language model with an external source of information. The term comes from a 2020 research paper by Lewis et al., “Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks” , which paired a pre-trained language model with a searchable index of Wikipedia. The retrieval step gives the model access to information stored outside its own parameters, which is why the approach supports fresher, domain-specific answers when the retrieval source is maintained and accessible.
Try this analogy: a standard LLM is a smart colleague answering from memory, and a RAG system is the same colleague with your company wiki open in another tab. The colleague is just as smart, but the answer is only as good as the wiki. If the wiki is outdated, disorganized, or missing pages, the answer reflects that.
That framing also tells your team where to focus. You can’t control the model, but you can improve the wiki. For marketers, the “wiki” includes your site, help center, documentation, and product pages.
RAG can affect answer engine optimization (AEO) because retrieval systems choose which passages to hand to the model, and clear, trustworthy passages are easier to use. Retrieval-friendly content uses clear structure, consistent terminology, and explicit facts, which improves machine accessibility and citation potential without guaranteeing citation.
Think about what a retrieval system does with a page. It splits the page into chunks and judges each chunk on its own. A chunk that opens with a direct answer, names the product or topic explicitly, and states facts in full sentences can stand alone. A chunk that says “as mentioned above, this is the best option” has lost its context.
This is also where AEO differs from traditional search. If you’re used to optimizing for rankings, our guide to AI SEO explains how the two approaches overlap and where they diverge. In short, ranking gets your page into a results list, while retrieval and citation determine whether an AI system uses your page inside an answer.
Keep in mind that answer engines differ. Some retrieve from the live web, some from curated indexes, and some from a company’s private documents. Citation behavior varies by platform and can change as products update. Treat any tactic as something that may improve your odds — then measure what happens.
Use RAG when your information changes often or when answers need to be traced back to sources. Use fine-tuning when you need to change how a model behaves, writes, or handles a specialized task. Turbine Kreuzberg’s RAG explainer is a useful outside reference for the retrieve, augment, generate flow and for this same comparison.
Limitations apply to both. RAG depends on retrieval quality, so a poorly organized knowledge base produces poor answers. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge in at a point in time, so it goes stale and needs retraining to update. Neither removes the need for human review, so the most effective approach is usually hybrid: the tool proposes, a person decides.
Start with this checklist. Each item makes your content easier for a retrieval system to find, interpret, and trust.
AI tools may never reach it. Lead each section with the answer, then add detail. A heading that asks a question, followed by a one- or two-sentence answer, gives a retrieval system a self-contained chunk to pull.
Use lists and short tables for comparisons and steps. Add a date and an author to pages where recency and expertise matter.

Customer-facing bots are one of the most common uses of this approach. For real-world context, see these examples of AI in customer service . Retrieval is also a core capability for more autonomous systems, and types of AI agents often rely on it to look up information before taking action.
Most RAG failures trace back to the content, not the model. Watch for these:
Hallucinations deserve special attention. A hallucination is when an AI generates false information with confidence. RAG reduces the risk by grounding answers in sources, but it doesn’t remove it.
A Stanford-led study published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies in 2025 tested RAG-based legal research tools whose vendors had promoted them as avoiding hallucinations. The researchers found that the tools from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters each hallucinated more than 17% of the time , although that rate was lower than that of a general-purpose chatbot. Retrieval helps, and human review is still required.
That review applies to AI-assisted content too. AI detection tools can flag text that looks machine-written, but they can’t tell you whether the facts in it are correct. Fact-checking stays a human job.
To keep your knowledge base reliable, set a few governance habits:
Here are the terms you’ll run into most, with what each means for your work. For more AI vocabulary, see our artificial intelligence glossary for marketers .
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): A technique that retrieves relevant information from an external source and gives it to a language model before it generates an answer. Marketing implication: your content can be the source.
Chunking: Splitting documents into smaller passages for storage and retrieval. Marketing implication: each section of your page may be judged on its own, so make sections self-contained.
Embeddings: Numerical representations of text that capture meaning, letting systems match related ideas even when the wording differs. Marketing implication: consistent terminology helps matching.
Vector database: A database that stores embeddings and finds the most similar ones quickly. Marketing implication: this is where prepared content often lives in a RAG system.
Augmentation: Adding retrieved material to the model’s prompt so it has context for its answer.
Citations: References that point to the sources behind an answer. Marketing implication: citations are how brands get credit and traffic from AI answers, though not every system provides them.
Hallucinations: False or fabricated information generated by an AI model. Marketing implication: accurate source content lowers the risk, and review catches what’s left.
Knowledge base: The collection of documents a RAG system retrieves from. Marketing implication: maintaining it is a content job as much as a technical one.
Context window: The amount of text a model can consider at once. Marketing implication: only a limited amount of retrieved material fits, so the most relevant chunks get priority.

None of this guarantees that an answer engine will retrieve or cite your content. It makes your content easier to work with and keeps your brand’s facts accurate wherever they’re used.
Once your content is in good shape, the next question is how your brand appears in AI answers today. HubSpot AEO shows marketers how their brand appears in AI-generated answers and which sources influence visibility. It also provides citation analysis and prioritized recommendations, which help marketers decide what to improve next.
Think of it as a way to monitor AI visibility, review the sources behind answers, and choose where to act first. It doesn’t make content RAG-ready on its own, and it can’t guarantee retrieval or citation. The content work described above still comes first.

Usually no. RAG systems retrieve from content you’ve already published or stored, so most teams don’t need a new CMS. What helps is clean structure, accurate metadata, and text that machines can read. If your CMS makes those hard to manage, such as locking content inside images or PDFs, that’s the part to fix.
Traditional SEO focuses on earning rankings in a list of search results. RAG is a method AI systems use to retrieve passages and build answers from them. The practices overlap, since clear structure and credible content help both, but the goal differs: SEO aims to earn clicks from rankings, while AEO aims to earn a place in the answer.
You can test by asking AI assistants questions, checking their answers, and checking which sources they cite. Because answers vary by platform and over time, a one-off check gives limited information. A dedicated tool such as HubSpot AEO can monitor how your brand appears and which sources shape the answers. Verify current plan availability and feature scope before relying on it.
Consider fine-tuning when you need a model to change its behavior, tone, or performance on a specialized task, and your information doesn’t change often. If your priority is fresh facts and answers tied to sources, RAG is usually the better fit. Many teams use both.
Audit your most important pages. Pick the ten topics that matter most to your business, find the page that should answer each one, and check whether it states the answer clearly, uses consistent terminology, and shows a current date. Fix those first, then assign an owner and review schedule to each page.
